chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
title: Speed Webb's band and McKinney's Cotton Pickers
summary: Crawford praises Speed Webb's swinging band with Roy Eldridge and wonders how McKinney's Cotton Pickers got Don Redman and Cuba Austin.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: Yes, I don't care what nobody say. I don't think -- well, other drummers and musicians have gone through the same things, you know, I imagine, but I didn't meet a lot of guys until I finally hit New York. There was a band, one of the swingingest bands I've

heard, myself, that Roy Eldridge played in. The name of the band was Speed Webb. I don't know whether you've heard of them. Maybe you did. Speed Webb had one of the swingingest bands in the land, but he -- he wasn't a New Yorker, came from out in the Middle West, Detroit or somewhere.

Roy Eldridge played with him, and Roy would say himself that that was one of the swingingest bands in the land. Of course, Speed, he liked to pose a lot up in front of the band, going into his posing and standing back. You know, he was a cutie, but he had a swinging band.

That McKinney's Cottonpickers, that's -- when Don Redmon was fronting that band, a heck of a band, McKinney's. Now, how in the world did McKinney come to manipulate and get great musicians in his band, Cubie Austin on drums. He did everything, great drummer. And he never fronted the band. Maybe he did when the band first started, but McKinney -- how did he maneuver, manipulate and get great guys like Don Redmon? He must have been paying pretty good money to arrange, write for the band and conduct it.

And we ran into Don, McKinney's Cottonpicker's band in Cleveland when we were there, naturally starving, stranded. But I can't figure this out, how he manipulated to get those great guys like Don Redmon. Don held forth at the Connie's Inn quite a time, you know, and good band. Old Big Sid.
